utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that -- good morning, everyone. I know that last week we'd indicated that it probably wouldn't be necessary for some small saving in terms of administrative economy to take the appearances each day, but since then there's been -- I've been advised that for the consistent accuracy of the transcript that I should ask for the appearances each -- at the beginning of each day. So if I may have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm Thomas Hannis on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. To my right is trial attorney Belinda Pidwell. From my near left to my far left are Alexis Demirdjian, legal officer; Gramsci Di Fazio, trial attorney; and our case manager, Crispian Smith. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours, Zecevic, Slobodan for Stanisic Defence. With me is Mr. Cvijetic, on my right; and on my left, Mr. O'Sullivan. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Igor Pantelic for Mr. Zupljanin. Next to me is my colleague co-counsel Mr. Dragan Krkovic. On my left is our legal assistant, attorney-at-law Brent Hicks; and next to him is Mr. Eric Tully, our case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we -- before we begin, there is something to which the Chamber would wish to draw the attention of the parties so that you may think about it and we will return to you for your views on our proposals at some point in the course of the next few days. That is that the trial will not sit on the 16th of October. And the Chamber proposes that to make up for this we will sit -- we will have extended hours on the 19th, 20th, and 21st. So if counsel could consider that, and we would return to inquire as to what views you have on the Chamber's proposal to make up that difference. Thank you. Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber has dealt with the Defence motion for the delay of testimony of Witness ST-019, and the Chamber saw fit to render an oral decision which is as follows: On 25th September, the Defence filed a joint motion seeking that the testimony of ST-019 be delayed by two months due to the Prosecution's disclosure on 23rd September of 29 documents totaling around 600 pages. The Prosecution responded on 28 September, and on the same date the Defence jointly sought leave to reply to the Prosecution's response, and they did file a reply. The Trial Chamber grants the Defence leave to file this reply. As a preliminary matter, the Trial Chamber notes that there are arguments in the Defence reply which the Defence could - and therefore should - have made in the Motion itself. The Chamber reminds the parties of their duty to bring all relevant arguments in motions. The alternative under Rule 126 bis is to file a reply with the leave of the Trial Chamber is not to be used to supplement arguments that the party forgot to include in its first original motion. This holds equally true in the situation such as the present where the parties have elected to enter into a quick exchange of submissions. The Trial Chamber notes the Prosecution's submission that it does not seek to rely on the 29 documents or to have them admitted into evidence and that the documents only contain references in passing by other persons to the witness himself, ST-019. While the material is disclosed pursuant to a request by the Defence, it is true, as the Defence argues, that the Prosecution disclose the documents very close to the testimony of ST-019. Nevertheless, in the circumstances of the present case, the Trial Chamber cannot find that the Prosecution has acted in breach of its obligation, nor does the Chamber find that the Defence is suffering any prejudice from hearing 019 today. Unless the documents for some reason are not included in the EDS system, then the Defence is able to search for and access the documents. The Defence is also free to call the witness to testify for the Defence if the material does turn out to have any significance. The joint Defence motion, therefore, is denied. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Is the Prosecution ready for the first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Di Fazio will be leading the first witness, ST-19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I, just before we bring in the witness, put a question. It appears that he's to testify in closed session. Is that correct? MR. DI FAZIO: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And would it make any sense to just check whether he still wants that, because the order for closed testimony was rendered a very long time ago in a situation where he was employed in a public service, and I understand that this is no longer the case. So we were just wondering whether we could perhaps relax the protective measures a bit. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, of course the Prosecution has no problem with the Trial Chamber making those inquiries if you wish to. However, I understand that he still remains and lives in an area of Bosnia that is predominantly of Serb ethnicity and he does hold concerns, I understand, that continue to this day. So unless there's been a substantial change in the circumstances that I'm not aware of and that he hasn't raised with me, the protective measures should continue. But of course if the Trial Chamber wants to raise it with him directly, then the Prosecution has no objection to that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We thought it might be worthwhile to raise with him at least perhaps not to abolish altogether the protective measures but just to relax them a bit so we could perhaps do -- MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I see no impediment, no reason why you shouldn't make that inquiry if the Trial Chamber feels that it should. Could we at least start that inquiry, though, in closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Absolutely. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: In that case, if Your Honours please, I'll call Witness ST-19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And so we move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Open session, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please, as a brief introduction to this witness, he testified in the past and, and he testified basically about events in Kotor Varos and his incarceration in Kotor Varos and events preceding the war and in the early part of the war in Kotor Varos, and that's the only introduction that I propose to give of his past testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness ST-19, did you testify at this Tribunal on the 16th and 17th of June 2003 in the Brdjanin case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yesterday were you provided with an opportunity to listen to an audio file of your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did have that opportunity, and I did listen to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to hear the questions of counsel and the answers that you gave to those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I listened to it in its entirety. I heard the questions from the Prosecutor and also questions from the Defence and my answers to the questions put.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you were to be examined on those same topics again today, would you provide that same testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My testimony would be identical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender into evidence the -- the Rule 92 ter statements of this witness, if that's necessary. I don't know if you propose to give them separate exhibit numbers, or whether under the terms of your order that you made it simply becomes part of the trial -- trial evidence. And I don't know whether you want to give the testimonies and statements that we hope to be adducing today and in the future separate exhibit numbers, P whatever. If it ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We would prefer to have them admitted as exhibits. MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly. If that's the case, then I ask that the two transcripts from the 16th and 17th of June, 2003, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If the counsel could kindly refer to the 65 ter number. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry. My apologies for that. The 65 ter number is 10004.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will become Exhibit P34 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was my understanding that the instruction from the Trial Chamber was that a part that -- parts of the statement or the transcripts which the Prosecution intends to rely on would be highlighted in -- in the documents in order to avoid the -- the enormous amount of material. That was my understanding of the principle that we were going to use in this case. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm just checking now as we -- if Your Honours would give me a moment to see that the -- yes. I see yellow on the exhibit. Yes, it's marked. The electronic file's marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. MR. DI FAZIO: It will have the yellow and the blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just needed this clarification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. We noted that it was marked. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to seek some clarification about various aspects of the testimony that you provided back in 2003. You provided a lot of evidence about events in your municipality, but I want you to turn your mind to events in June of 1992, and in fact, the period of time soon after Bajram in June of 1992. In your evidence you describe some attacks on villages around Kotor Varos, and you describe the movements of villagers who were congregating at various locations in other villages, and you describe your own movements. Eventually you describe going to a place called Plitska, and eventually from Plitska going off to negotiate with Serb forces. And you say that you went with two other gentlemen whose name I don't need to mention now. And you describe being stopped by policemen wearing blue uniforms. Can you remember how many policemen stopped you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the bridge of the Bosanka River we were stopped by a group of young men. Some of them were in blue uniforms of the reserve police forces in Yugoslavia, a uniform that was well known to me. Some of them were in camouflage uniforms. It was a group of five to seven young men. I can't really say the exact number. Of course I knew all of those young men because these were all people from the neighbourhood. The last names were Djuric, Krezovic, Tepic, and so on. It was a group of five to seven men. Some of them were in reserve police uniforms and some were in camouflage uniforms or partially camouflage and partially civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the policemen who were dressed in blue uniforms, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the other men who weren't in blue uniform, the who were dressed this camouflage uniform or partially camouflage in civilian clothing, can you tell us, if you know - and tell us if you don't know - but can you tell us if you know if there were members of any armed formation such as the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were armed. I don't know which formations they belonged to. That's something I really cannot say with certainty. I assume that these were people who belonged to units of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what had been your intention as you approached these -- these men who were armed and in uniform? What had you been hoping to achieve by going down to this place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I expected that was the intention, and my assignment was with two companions who were accompanying me to set up -- or to establish contacts with Mr. Slobodan Zupljanin and to possibly have talks and possibly agree about the possibility of stopping any kind of combat actions and to find some sort of solution about what to do with the population, how to take the population out. The wish was to help people in some way and to prevent further escalation of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you and your two companions armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you and your two companions members of the police or in any armed group, members of an armed group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not members of any military formation, neither of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony back in June of 2003, you further describe being taken after your arrest to the Maslovare primary school. Were your two companions also arrested and taken to the place? By that I mean the two men who accompanied you down to -- to the point where you -- where you were arrested.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were with me as far as a catering facility in the centre of Vrbanjci where we met Mr. Zupljanin, Slobodan Zupljanin. His nickname was Bebac. Of course then they were separated from me in this cafe. That's where they were separated from me, and I was taken in a civilian van with some other people who had been brought there to the primary school in Maslovare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the people who were taken with you to the primary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The group that was taken with me in that van were all Muslims. In Maslovare, in the primary school we saw that there were some Croats there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've described in your evidence that people congregated and kept in a room at Maslovare, the primary school. What was the ethnicity of those people? Were they all Croats, or were there other ethnicities there as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats were there, Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you were taken from the point of your arrest, the place where you were arrested, the place where you saw those men, those policemen in the blue uniform, to Maslovare Primary School, were you escorted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were soldiers in camouflage uniforms. Some of them had white cross belts, and I assume that they were members of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So do I -- do I understand -- tell me if this is correct: You were -- you were escorted from the point of arrest to the Maslovare Primary School by soldiers. Is that correct? Not policemen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, soldiers, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Do you know -- well, you testified in June of 2003 that you know a gentleman maimed Savo Tepic. How long had you known that man in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Savo Tepic and I have known each other from childhood. We went to the same primary school. We were born in the same local commune. Perhaps there's an age difference of three or four years between us. And we also graduated in mechanical engineering, and we worked in the same company. I worked there until the 11th of June, and before that Mr. Tepic had taken on the post of the chief of police of Kotor Varos after the local elections there -- or, rather, after the parliamentary elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your evidence you describe eventually being taken from Maslovare Primary School to the police station. Perhaps before I get to the police station I should ask you the manner in which you were taken out of Maslovare Primary School. Was everyone in the room taken away or just yourself or a selection of individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there was a period in the morning when we were called out and taken out. Myself and a young man who was a Croat - his name was Marijan Miskic, were taken out from the facility. There was a vehicle waiting for us. I think it was a civilian and not a military vehicle. And the two of us were taken with handcuffs from the Maslovare Elementary School to the police station in Kotor Varos. Just the two of us, myself and Mr. Marijan Miskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And the other people who had been in the room with you, they were left behind at Maslovare; correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they stayed at Maslovare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who - tell us, if you know - who transported you or escorted you from Maslovare to the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the names of the people. In any case, these were young men who were known to me. The only person whom I knew well from before was Mr. Nebojsa Sebic. He was in a soldier's camouflage uniform, and judging by the quality of the uniform and his conduct, he must have been some sort of senior officer in the military formation that was stationed at that school at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any policemen in the group or who escorted you from Maslovare to the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mostly soldiers. There was no one there from the civilian police. I assume since one of the young men had white cross belts on and a white belt that he was a member of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified about arriving at the police station. The first night that you were at the police station, did you see Savo Tepic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the corridor while it was still not known which room we would be placed in on the floor, I did see Mr. Tepic in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Doing the best you can, was that when you first arrived there or later in the evening? Can you recall? Later in the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just when we came. We were still not placed anywhere. We were still in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What -- what sort of condition were you in at the time that Savo Tepic -- that you saw Savo Tepic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in handcuffs in some sort of sorry state. I was afraid. There was beating on the way. In any case, it was a very ugly picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about your companion, the young Croatian man? What sort of condition was he in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan Miskic was in even a worse state than myself. As he was being brought in he was beaten, and he looked much worse than I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did either of you have any blood on your clothing or on your faces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The clothes were wet. There was nonstop rain in the course of those few days, and they were dirty. We were quite a mess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And from -- when you saw Mr. Tepic, can you tell us, again doing the best you can, if he would have been in a position to see you and your Croatian companion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I sincerely hoped, giving my previous relationship with Mr. Tepic, I secretly hoped for some protection, but it was my impression that Mr. Tepic completely ignored us as if we didn't exist and as if he did not see us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks for that, but notwithstanding what you hoped for, just tell us this: Was Mr. Tepic in a position to see you and your Croatian companion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. It's a corridor. There were no other people there save for those escorting us and the two of us. Certainly he could see us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your evidence you describe a couple of visits that you made out of the prison that you were later kept in. One was to the workers' university and the other one was to Banja Luka. I want to ask you about the Banja Luka visit. You described being taken out of the police station and taken to Banja Luka, I think the next day after you were first taken to the police station. Who took you from Kotor Varos to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A civilian Golf car was used. The driver was a gentleman whom I had known somewhat. I learned his first and last name only later. It was Zdravko Samardzija. He wore a camouflage uniform with a camouflage hat which resembled a cowboy hat. Escorting us was Mr. Vlado Novakovic, a young man whom I had known well previously. He wore a reserve police uniform, that is to say, a blue one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. And about Mr. Samardzija. Can you tell the Trial Chamber if he was a member of the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met Mr. Samardzija then at that time. He took us to Banja Luka and returned us back to the police station and to the prison in Kotor Varos. We never met afterwards. I don't know what military formation he belonged to, but in any case he wore the uniform I described, a camouflage uniform with a camouflage hat resembling a cowboy hat. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown 65 ter 2142, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This building should be the police building in Banja Luka, in Marsala Tita Street, across the road from the court in Banja Luka. On the right-hand side of the picture there should be the school of electrical engineering and the Ferhadija. I think Mr. Samardzic brought us to this building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a CSB building or an SJB building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that the acronym CSB is unclear. I suppose it's the centre of security services. In any case, I don't know. It was a police building. It had been a police building prior to the war in Banja Luka. I had never been in that building. This was the only occasion, and thank God it was the last. I never visited the building before that, although I do know that it was a police building. I suppose it was sort of a central building for the police in Banja Luka. All other police stations that I was aware of were far smaller and modest in appearance. I suppose this would be the principal police building in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. You describe in your evidence being taken there and suffering some light blows and threatening gestures. Were you kept in the one place in the building, or were you taken around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in only one room. In the room next door there was the young man who was brought in with me, that is to say Marijan Miskic. We were in separate rooms. In any case, I was in only one room. The only times during which I left the room was to go to the toilet, and I was always escorted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your evidence you describe later catching up with Mr. Miskic and being taken back to -- back to Kotor Varos. And you describe him having broken ribs. Had he -- did he have broken ribs before he went to the police, to this place, or did he sustain those injuries there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that in this building I was not physically mistreated. In the room next door one could hear constant shouting, moaning, and noise. He was frequently taken out to the toilet. When we met again, he could not walk in a normal fashion. He did complain of pain in his ribs. Even the gentleman who was bringing us back said something to the extent that if he is in that much pain because of the ribs, he should be allowed to see a doctor. As a result of that beating, Mr. Miskic suffered a lot, because for a long time after that, in the Kotor Varos building -- prison, he could not move about. He was a young man who had previously been quite fit, but once he returned, he spent a lot of time simply lying on the ground since he could not move about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And just to finish up with this topic. Looking at that photograph, is the room that you were taken to shown in the photograph anywhere by any chance, or is it not visible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot go into such detail. I really don't know. I know that we were taken up to a floor, but I don't know to which room. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender that image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Tendered, admitted, and marked with the next number in the series.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P35, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. In your evidence from June 2003, you describe at considerable length your imprisonment until the 23rd of July, 1993. You were kept in the same prison throughout that year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout that period I was in the same prison, until the New Year's, I think, when we were transferred from the room number 3 to a larger and better equipped room which was closer to the entrance. Therefore, I did not move out of the prison. I was not transferred anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the ethnicity of your fellow prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the prison there were detainees of Muslim and Croat background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to give the Trial Chamber an idea of what exactly this building was. And let's start with its pre-war use. What had this place been used for prior to the outbreak of war in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a member of the reserve force of the JNA, I used to go to that building to be issued with military equipment that was due to the military -- to the reserve force. I know that that building used to be a TO warehouse during the Yugoslav times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had the building ever been used as part of the formal prison system existing in Bosnia prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether anyone served their sentence in that prison before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had it been used for TO purposes prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how long. I do know that it was used. For example, as I was serving my military term in the 1980s, it was used for that purpose. I don't know whether it was used to that end prior to that period. I never actually entered the building at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know a gentleman named Zdravko Pejic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had known Mr. Pejic from earlier times. I think my first ID when I turned 18 was issued to me in Kotor Varos by him. That's how I know him as a police employee. He also appeared there during our time of detention. He frequently visited the prison. I think he was a person who had the authority to enter the prison at any time. He even issued certain orders to those securing the prison. During my stay in the prison, I frequently saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a policeman during 1992 when you were in prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zdravko Pejic usually arrived in a camouflage uniform, but it was a blue camouflage uniform, not an SMB uniform. By that time one could already see people in blue camouflage uniforms. This was a novelty for us. We didn't even know such uniforms existed, because by that time we had grown accustom to the SMB camouflage uniforms. It was my presumption, therefore, that he was a police employee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. During the time that you were incarcerated, did you meet or come to know a gentleman with the surname Zaric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a young man who had been a policeman in Croatia prior to the war there. That man also commanded the policemen in the early period, in June and July, who were securing the prison. He commanded the group of policemen who manned the gate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Prosecutor, may I remind you that you have used 35 minutes as of this moment. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I regret my underestimate. I've just about wrapped it up, though, so I'm hopeful in finishing in the next minute or two. Thank you. Thank you for that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, the last name I want to put to you is a gentleman bearing the surname Krejic. Did you know anyone in 1992 whilst in prison with the surname Krejic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At a given time a group of prisoners was taken out for work. These detainees were Croats, and one of them, I think his name was Sipura escaped. It is then that the entire structure in the prison was replaced. Therefore, this Krejic man whom I had known since before the war, replaced Mr. Zaric as the commander of the police force securing the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question is this. Just moments ago you said that -- talking about the man you knew as Mr. Zaric, that he commanded the policemen in the early period in June and July who were securing the prison. Did police secure the prison throughout your incarceration, or is it just in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout my period of incarceration in the Kotor Varos prison, it was the police who secured the prison. Of course they rotated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Prosecutor. And we will now, as I told you, pass the floor on to the two Defence teams, and the first counsel who is going to cross-examine you will be Mr. Zecevic, who is representing the accused Mico Stanisic, and Mr. Zecevic has asked for 40 minutes for his cross-examination of you, and we will grant him that. Thereafter, Mr. Pantelic, who is representing the other accused, Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, will proceed with his cross-examination, and Mr. Pantelic has asked for one hour, and we will give him that. After the cross-examination of the two Defence teams, we might ask the Prosecution if they have any short re-examination questions to put to you, and when they have completed their questions maybe the Judges on the bench will have some extra questions for you, and that will then conclude your testimony for today. I give the floor to Mr. Zecevic with -- and 40 minutes to complete his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. In your statement, you say that Kotor Varos, prior to the war, was a poor and -- poorly developed municipality in Bosnia, much as the rest of the Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The association of municipalities of Bosanska Krajina was formed back in the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The municipality -- the association of municipalities of the Bosanska Krajina, including Kotor Varos, was formed prior to 1990.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You acted as vice-president of the SDA in Kotor Varos. All different ethnic political parties were represented in that municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know a precise date of its formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about a year? 1990, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that I don't know it precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know when the HVO was formed, the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know precisely. I don't know when the HVO was formed, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian national party, the HDZ, had its own political structure in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You are aware that the HVO had units in the area of the municipality of Kotor Varos at the latest by September 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of any HVO units, and I don't know whether -- I don't know when they were formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You are probably familiar with the fact that the Crisis Staff of the HDZ was formed as early as March 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know when the HDZ Crisis Staff was formed, but in my previous testimony I had an opportunity to go through some of the minutes of a body called like that. It was part of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the Crisis Staff of the HDZ was formed in early March 1992, or do you require to see a document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You don't need to do that. I suppose such a body was functioning, and since I did see some of their minutes, I -- as evidence, I suppose that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When did the SDA establish its Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what the date would be precisely. It involved certain incidents and barricades along the main road. This in a way was a reason to have a meeting at the municipal level of the party. I presume it was in the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, as of spring 1992, both the HDZ and the SDA had their respective Crisis Staffs in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You know, don't you, that the HDZ initiate the erection of barricades in February and early March in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know of the barricades. They came about as a result of an incident, that is to say, a wounding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please just answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was the HDZ who initiated that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have, please, 4002, 1D4002, on the e-court, please. 4002. Your Honours, I need your instructions. It has been uploaded and released as far as we're concerned. We checked that with the technicians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If you have a hard copy --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- then we can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have the first page put on the ELMO, please. The lower part. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, can you see the document? It bears the date of the 6th of March. In the last paragraph a certain Janja Mandic says: "We made a mistake concerning the barricades."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can I just ask a question to counsel? Since we don't read B/C/S very well, could you please explain to us what this document is and where it comes from?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is -- the document, of course, has a translation that's -- I'm sorry, but this is a technical glitch. This is a document -- this is the minutes of the HDZ Crisis Staff meeting held on the 6th of March, 1992, where they're discussing the barricades where they are -- which they erected, and they are saying that obviously they made a mistake. I'm just trying to help witness -- witness's recollection. If he knows, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to answer your question about the barricades. I am not familiar with this document. I can only be aware of such minutes if presented to me by the OTP or Defence. This -- these are minutes of a group of Croats of whom I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just first a -- I was just informed that the document is in e-court. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, my question was this: Are you aware of the fact that the HDZ and Croats erected barricades around the 5th of March in Kotor Varos, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who organised that. I do know, however, that there were barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you talk about the Patriotic League and the Green Berets as illegal paramilitary organisations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These were, so to say, the military factions of the SDA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean in general or only in the territory of Kotor Varos municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when these military factions or wings of the SDA were formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 1991 perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the area of Kotor Varos, some say that over 1 million German marks were spent for arms in the area of Vecici and Vrbanjci in early 1992. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that money. I'm not aware that such a high sum of money was spent for arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You know Sadikovic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Mr. Sadikovic as of the time when the SDA was being formed in the municipality. He was also assigned a position in the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "position," do you mean his tasks in the organisation and arming of Muslims in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I have in mind his position as the deputy commander of the police in the Kotor Varos police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you disagreed with Mr. Sadikovic on the issue of creation of the Muslim TO and the arming and organising of the Muslims living in Kotor Varos Municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know him well before that time. Given the fact that our party could appoint a leading person in the police as a result of the elections, then that position being commander or deputy commander, it was given to Mr. Sadikovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I pray you -- you know we are limited in terms of time, please answer my question. Is it correct that within the SDA you and Mr. Sadikovic had diverging views on the issue of organising, arming, and establishing a Muslim TO as well as its illegal process of arming? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were certain things that we disagreed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After you were detained, you were interrogated by the State Security Service as a suspect, someone who allegedly took part in an armed rebellion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, 33, 11, it's "armed rebellion," not "around rebellion."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You recall having given at least two statements to the State Security Service, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit 1D3994 on the e-court. Your Honours, I'm sorry I missed -- because of the technical glitch, I missed the previous document to be asked to be admitted as an exhibit, the previous document which we found eventually on the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm -- just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just give us one moment, please. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we reluctantly agree that the document should be admitted. Our reservation is based on the fact that the witness, whereas he has alluded to it, he can't speak directly about the contents of the document. He wasn't the -- it is something that puts a bit of a context to what he's saying, what it is -- he is neither the maker nor he is -- you get what I'm saying. But we do understand the relevance, and it is for that limited reason that we agree that it should be admitted as an exhibit. But the documents such as this in the future, we would respectfully remind you to -- that they wouldn't -- that they can't be admitted as of right, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand and I appreciate, Your Honour. Your Honours, I have a problem with the -- with the next two documents because they are not redacted, and the witness's name appear on them. So I would like your instruction -- MR. DI FAZIO: And it also appears on this particular document as well, on the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Which document, the one -- MR. DI FAZIO: The one that was just admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: So I don't know. I think redactions might be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If the witness's name appeared on the last document, it needs to be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D1 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, did or did not the name appear? MR. DI FAZIO: I understood that it might have been -- the document might have had a camera on it and the name might have gone out to the wider public. I'm informed by my colleagues. Would Your Honours just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm also sorry, Your Honours. I believe we've already introduced some documents. I'm pretty sure with it, so this cannot be 1D1. MR. DI FAZIO: No, the previous document, there was not a name. I made a mistake; I apologise. It's on the current document that the name appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honours, the document is indeed 1D6, and it should not be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can we go into the private session so I can present these redacted statements to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm being told that we need not go into private session, but what we can do is that we can make sure that the documents are not exhibited to the public or shown to the public. So we can stay where we are in open session, but we will prevent documents from being --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- transmitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can the witness please be shown document 3994.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Can the witness be shown the last page with his signature, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, is this your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to read it in its entirety, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If Your Honours would like me to provide the -- the hard copy, maybe it's easier for the witness to ... Your Honours, I hope this is not affecting my time. I'm really sorry, but there is nothing I can do about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was: Do you recognise this as your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the statement, and it contains the elements. I do recall some details. Yes, this is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you talk about this conflict with Sadikovic -- or, rather, the differences of opinion with Sadikovic, who was in favour of arming and the forming of the TO, illegal arming, thus which you were against. It's clear -- it was clear to you then that something like that constitutes an armed rebellion, doesn't it not -- was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that is why you were of the opinion that this should not be done, because this would provoke inter-ethnic or international conflicts in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout the entire conflict, I wanted to seek ways to find a peaceful solution or a solution by peaceful means.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the statement witness has recognised as his own, and I would move the Trial Chamber to admit it into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Tendered, admitted, and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D7 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown the document 3990. It's another of his statements, and I'm providing the hard copy to the witness so he can refresh his memory. The document is in the e-court 3990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you recognise this -- this statement as yours? This is a supplement -- supplemental statement to the one we looked at before of the 20th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is my statement, but if you permit me, I think that I was interviewed only once in the sense of an investigation previously in -- about the matters in that building in Banja Luka. I don't recall giving a statement on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the signature. Is it your signature in that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you are saying, this is my statement, this is my signature, but I do not recall when I provided it," but you do allow for the possibility that this is your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours can I move the Trial Chamber to admit this statement as he recognised his signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D8, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, would you be good enough to explain to us what the evidence is that you wish us to extract from this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this is -- in these two statements the witness is talking about -- about his disagreement with Mr. Sadikovic in -- within the Party of Democratic Action in Kotor Varos where Mr. Sadikovic and some other persons were organising the -- the Muslim TO and illegal arming and organisation of the military organisation, like basically an armed rebellion. And for the purposes of this trial, I think it's very relevant since the witness was arrested based on his alleged taking part in the armed rebellion and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honours. Exhibit 1D8 should be under seal, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, during the examination-in-chief by my colleague the Prosecutor, on page 25, lines 5 to 7, you talked about serving in the military and being in the JNA reserves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did serve the military term of duty, and I was in the reserve forces of the Kotor Varos TO detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Territorial Defence as part of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me the equipment that you were issued from the TO warehouse. Did you keep it at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't keep the equipment at home. During the previous two years I was more engaged on work duties, and I was not issued with equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... take a break now. It's 90 minutes, so we will adjourn -- in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have probably five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Registrar, how much time has counsel have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I've been told that you have five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry, there was a mistake. The Registrar is re-checking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe, according to my calculation, at least 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we will have the break now. The Registrar informs me that you have ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But we might grant you an extra five minutes. Thank you. We will adjourn and come back at five minutes past half 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could you please push the button, and also the security officer. And Mr. Zecevic, would you be helpful. Okay, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Everything is coming down at the same moment, Your Honours. I'm saying that everything is coming down at the same moment, so there is no need for me to push another button.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It was just -- it was just to save time so that the usher didn't have to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we are given to understand that you have a concern as to the amount of time you have left to complete your cross-examination. According to our record-keeping, the 40 minutes that you had indicated earlier that you would have required, that you have, give or take, eight minutes that have remaining. Now, we appreciate that our calculations may not have accounted for the procedural issues which would have arisen, but how much more time do you now think that you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I said Your Honour -- I said to Your Honours, probably you didn't understand me, that I would be able to finish in five minutes. But I was just concerned because we gave -- we gave two hours for the whole four witnesses, and that is why I'm concerned about the time, because we might need to cross-examine another witness for a longer period of time, and that is why I'm concerned if -- if procedural matters are accounted against my time. That's -- that was the only thing that I raised with the -- with the Registry. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But immediately in terms of this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In terms of this witness five minutes more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we don't have a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, we don't have a problem with this witness. No, no, I'm just -- I was just referring to the general requirement of two hours which I requested, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, before the break we talked about the fact that you were in the reserve TO of the JNA and that you were not issued with any equipment. When I said "equipment," I met a uniform. You were not even issued a uniform, or were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember if I had a uniform at my apartment or not, but just the uniform, no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Just the uniform. This is what I would like to know. If you do not recall if you had one, do you know anyone who did have uniforms issued to them which they kept at their home or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People who were going to the front in Croatia, who had responded to the mobilisation, mostly did have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking generally about the reserve forces, the JNA reservists. I'm not talking about the 1990s, I'm generally speaking from the time that you had completed your term of duty in the JNA armed forces in the 1980s or 1980. After that you were transferred to the reserves just like many others, and when you were transferred to the reserve forces you should have been issued a uniform which you were supposed to take home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was issued with a uniform from the reserve forces, but as far as I can recall the last two years, because my work duties, I was released from the TO unit, and I was supposed to return the uniform, which is, I think, what I did sometime in 1989, perhaps, or 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we clarified this. This referred to you because of the specific nature of your work duties, but the others had their uniforms at home, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, when you were arrested and when you stayed in all of those places where you stayed, people were dressed in different uniforms. You referred to camouflage uniforms, olive-grey uniforms, reserve forces, olive-grey uniforms, a combination civilian clothing and uniforms, camouflage uniforms that were blue, police uniforms, some cowboy hats. What I'm trying to say is that during the time that you were arrested and held in all of those places, people appeared in all kinds of uniforms, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On my way from Vrbanjci to Maslovare and on the way back to the Kotor Varos police station, I did see people who were dressed in that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If -- so you would agree with me that the uniforms people were wearing did not indicate that they were members of a particular unit. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would not be able to say to which military formations they belonged, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 27 of the transcript, lines 6 and 7, in response to a question by the Prosecutor whether the police was securing that prison where you were, which was actually a TO depot, you said that "during the period that I spent in the Kotor Varos prison, it was the police that was guarding that prison, and they rotated." But what you know, actually, is that these were persons who were wearing some sort of police uniforms. You don't actually know that they were police officers or policemen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that they wore police uniforms, and the two persons referred to by name, I knew that previously they worked in the police station as policemen up until the incident. I am thinking of Mr. Krejic and Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But you do allow for the possibility that they were mobilised into some military formation at that particular point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, such a -- such a possibility does exist. I'm talking about their uniforms and their previous duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have one more question. When we spoke about the uniforms that the reservists of the TO and the JNA kept at home, the same applied to the reserve policemen, did it not? They also kept their police uniforms, the reserve police uniforms, at home, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not belong to such a formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No other exhibits. I was just checking out if I have something. Thank you very much. Your Honours, there is one matter which -- which we would need to raise. Maybe it would be proper when the -- when the witness leaves, because it's housekeeping matter. We just need to clarify something with the exhibits from -- from previous cases. Is that okay, or do you want me to raise it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Does it affect this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does affect this witness, but it's matter on the -- well, I can say. Basically the Prosecution tendered his transcripts from the other cases. Now -- from Brdjanin case, I believe, and there is a number of -- of exhibits in that -- in that transcript. So does these exhibits become part of our exhibit list? If they are, they have to have the numbers. I'm just wondering what is the situation about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the Chamber issued an order yesterday -- or a decision, sorry, in which we admitted into evidence the transcripts of this witness's testimony in earlier cases, the case against Brdjanin being one of them, in which this witness testified. In doing so, we also admitted those exhibits that were tendered through this witness at the Brdjanin trial and the other trials. That is to say those exhibits which appears -- which appear on the Prosecution's 65 ter list, again the idea being that we simply do not wish to admit anything that has not appeared on the Prosecution's 65 ter list. So that's the answer to your question. So those exhibits that did appear on the Prosecution's 65 ter list and that were tendered through this witness in his early testimonies in other cases have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, with all due respect, how are we going to refer to those exhibits? They should have exhibit number in this case. We can't call them whatever, 1D375 from Brdjanin. They have to have a number in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But how are we going to deal with that? That was the essence of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I need to bring this to your attention, because this -- this was an issue that was -- was discussed during some of our pre-trial proceedings, and I frankly have to confess that I don't know that it was ever completely clearly resolved. We had taken the position that for those 92 ter witnesses, when there were prior transcripts that made references to exhibits that were admitted or shown to those witnesses in that testimony should be part of the 92 ter package that you as the triers of fact would want to have in order to fully understand their testimony without the necessity of giving each of those separate exhibit numbers. And because we were taking that position, I think for a lot of these 92 ter prior transcripts and prior statements where perhaps specific exhibits had been discussed in the written statements. They were shown, identified by an ERN, and discussed by the witness. I think a large number of those are not on our 65 ter exhibit list that was filed at the time we filed our pre-trial brief. Because we viewed those sort of in the same way we view expert reports, that it's included within that package so that you can have an understanding of the transcript. I think Mr. Zecevic raises a good point. If we're going to have those exhibits be in evidence in this case, they do get a number. And you'll also need a key because Exhibit P113 in Brdjanin will be 65 ter number 912 in this case, and we'll get a P number that's going to be different than the Brdjanin number or the Krajisnik number or the Milosevic number, whatever case the transcript comes from. And we would like you to have those exhibits to put the testimony in context and read it. Now, a number of the exhibits that are of particular importance to us, of course, are on our 65 ter list and will be introduced otherwise. But, frankly, I don't know how to deal that -- deal with that, and I wanted to bring it to your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Trial Chamber and senior legal officer and registrar confer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis and Mr. Di Fazio --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- and Counsels, let me be clear if I can about the policy of admission of documents into evidence that we have chosen in this trial. The policy is that documents outside the parties' 65 ter lists are not admissible. In other words, we simply do not wish to deal with documents that we cannot find in the parties' 65 ter list respectively. Now, you have a great number of documents already in your 65 ter list. If you wish to see other documents admitted into evidence, then please move to have them included in your list. And when the comes to the two Defence counsels, then the advice is the same for you. The Chamber will not consider documents -- or admission of documents that are not included in your 65 ter lists. That's the first issue. The second issue about the numbering of those exhibits that came in by our decision yesterday, we do not at this moment have a full overview of exactly how many documents it was, so what we propose to do, just for now, is to say that these exhibits that came in through our decision yesterday will be given exhibit numbers, and that the way we'll do it is that we'll have the transcripts given an exhibit number, and then the adjacent documents that came in through the witness's testimony in that transcript will then be given decimal numbers, that is to say, exhibit number so-and-so, .1, .2, .3, and so on so that we can find the relevant documents relating to the witness's testimony as it appears in that particular transcript. I think that's the smartest and the simplest way to go ahead. So what we will do, we will ask the court officer to consult with the parties after this hearing and then sort out the issue of numbering. And maybe tomorrow or maybe on the next time we have a hearing, then we will just use five minutes to read those exhibit numbers into the record. So for now, Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Pantelic, if you would be good enough to refer to the 65 ter numbers, the e-court numbers, for these documents if you wish to use them now, but they don't have an exhibit number yet, but they will be given exhibit numbers very soon. So until they're given exhibit numbers, please just use the other e-court numbering systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, just one -- just one -- one thing. As I understood Mr. Hannis just two minutes ago, a number of these exhibits which are admitted by your decision yesterday pertaining to this witness and his testimony in the previous cases are not on the 65 ter list of the OTP. So therefore, how will they become exhibits in this case if they're not on the 65 ter list? I mean, I think this is in a -- in a clear contradiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: By asking the Chamber for leave to have them admitted into their 65 ter list, and then we'll have a look at it, and we'll decide whether or not they can be admitted into the 65 ter list and from there into exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. So first they have to ask to amend their 65 ter list. And that brings me to another issue, I mean which is very similar. This is the issue which we raised about the experts. The expert reports contain the number of exhibits which are not on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: May I suggest that we keep this discussion at a later time when we can take some time off to deal with household matters --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- and that we proceed with the witness for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I just wanted to put the Trial Chamber on notice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before I begin, I would propose, if it's convenient for witness to have B/C/S version of his previous statement to OTP so that we can go through particular parts if necessary. So, Ms. Usher, please can I have your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution has no objection? MR. DI FAZIO: These are the written -- written and signed statements of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. We got it -- it's a B/C/S version that we got from you in disclosure procedure, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I have no objection to prior statements being put to the witness, but it seems to me that perhaps the -- Mr. Pantelic should elicit whatever evidence he wants, and if he's got any problem with the evidence he wants and then wants to make use of a prior statement, that would be the normal procedure. Otherwise, in itself it shouldn't be used at this stage. He should just cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's a matter just in case that witness needs some refreshment of his memory for certain parts, that we shall not lost -- losing our time. That's the point. MR. DI FAZIO: I appreciate that, and I'm always grateful to make up time, but the witness hasn't been asked anything yet. We don't know if he's got any memory problems, and if he does and it becomes necessary for him to refer to his statement, that's the point at which it should be produced, not at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, we understand counsel for the Prosecution's - and I mean no disrespect when I say - technical objection. But for convenience we understand that it would be practical for the witness to have the document now, but remember it is only being used as the occasion arises as your questioning proceeds when you have to -- whether he has to refresh his memory at a particular point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. That was my goal. Thank you so much. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry, this is the one dated the -- October 1996 and May 1997. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. My name is Mr. Pantelic, attorney-at-law. I represent Mr. Zupljanin. You have had previous experience with the testimony in this court, therefore you know the procedure. When I put a question to you, you should wait for a few moments before answering to assist the interpreters, to have a precise transcript, and to have everything conveyed. So I kindly ask you, just pause briefly before answering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Witness, you were one of the founders of the SDA in Kotor Varos; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was. I was one of the founders of the SDA in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, it suffices to say yes or no at this stage. We can move more quickly that way. Mr. Muhamed Sadikovic was also one of the founders of the SDA in Kotor Varos; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sadikovic was one of the founders of the SDA in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask you again to say yes or no only. Do you know Dr. Mirza Mujacic [phoen]from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Mr. Mujacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He was the president of the regional SDA board with its seat in Prijedor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You frequently met with Mr. Mujacic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not frequently. On several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Prijedor is further away from Banja Luka than Kotor Varos is; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was the reason to have the seat for the Regional Board for the entire Krajina in Prijedor rather -- rather than in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not certain that the seat was in Prijedor. In any case, meetings were frequently held in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muharem Krzic and Mr. Bajazit Jahic, were they also members of the Regional Board of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for Bajazit Jahic, I am not certain; and I think Mr. Krzic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Muhamed Sadikovic was one of the authors of a book called "To Testify to Crimes and Bosnian Patriotism"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have never read that book, but I have heard of its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Muhamed Krzic was one of the authors of the book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that in that book Mr. Sadikovic spoke in detail about the preparations for armed conflicts in the territory of Kotor Varos municipality, you would agree with me that that fact is true.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I fail to understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe it's a matter of translation. I'll try to be more succinct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that book Mr. Sadikovic speaks in detail about the preparation for the arming of Muslim and Croat members in Kotor Varos Municipality, does he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not read the book, and I don't know what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss that with any friends of yours? Did you discuss the contents of the book since you were a prominent member of that community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that several people whose names can be found in the book were dissatisfied with seeing their names in the book at all. They came to me to ask me for my opinion. I personally have no opinion about the quality of that book. I never found it necessary to actually read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sadikovic was the commander of that military formation in Kotor Varos Municipality, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned of him being commander upon my release from prison. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, it's not clear to me what military formation we're talking about, unless I've missed something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about that Muslim unit in the territory of Kotor Varos Municipality, aren't we? MR. DI FAZIO: I've still got a problem with that. No problem with the line of questioning, but it's just got to be absolutely clear. Are we talking about a SDA Muslim unit? What precisely are we talking about here, because it could be any nature of animal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, we are discussing a military unit with Muslim members. This was not exclusively a party unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood, Counsel, and the party was not mentioned in the context of the unit, and I don't think you attempted to allude at that -- to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Precisely, Witness. Tell me, before your arrest, what was your position per some organisational plan that you should have been assigned to in that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that I was one of the few whose war experience and work experience was unrelated to that. I belonged to no military formation until the 11th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In your statement you say that you are well-versed in explosives and mines; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My JNA military service was in the field of engineering and explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As part of that training, sabotage personnel are also experts in the field of mines and explosives; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the reserve force of the JNA in Kotor Varos Municipality, I was assigned to a sabotage reconnaissance unit. My military -- based on my military speciality from the JNA during my time of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are a reserve officer. I understand what you are talking about, but we should have this explained for the transcript and the Chamber. The acronym VES, V-E-S, that means that you have been trained in a certain military speciality; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a JNA term.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: From your statement I can see that you're exceptionally versed in the different types of weapons. For example, you discuss a Thompson rifle on page 4, paragraph 2, of your statement. Next, a PAP or semi-automatic rifle is mentioned as well as a light machine-gun, M-72, which is found on page 7, paragraph 2, of your statement. The same page, number 7, you mention PM-84, which is a heavy machine-gun, in paragraph four. Sorry, page 8, paragraph 2, since there are differences between the versions. Next you mention mortars, recoilless guns, and artillery, on page 10, paragraph 1. Therefore, you have an exceptional knowledge about the types of weapons. At least that is what I conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I served my military term with the JNA, and I was decorated as an exceptional serviceman, which at that time was a very highly valued commendation. As for the structure and weapons of the JNA, this is something I was well acquainted with as a soldier at that time.
