Regarding the specific types of weapons, during the war in Croatia such weapons appeared in the territory of Kotor Varos municipality as war booty or through some other channels. It was mainly reservists who sported such weapons which belonged to the arsenal of the JNA and were of the Crvena Zastava make. I know that much, but I wouldn't say that I'm exceptionally well-versed in weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you have information about a large quantity of explosives, TNT explosives that was seized on the border between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina? There were some 15 tons of explosive seized on that occasion. Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At which border crossing?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Brod.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I seem to recall something that was published in the media. This seems to have been an incident and that explosives were being transported. I don't know any more detail than that. This is what I could learn from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are familiar with the name of Miro Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I know Mr. Miro Petrusic as an active-duty policeman in Kotor Varos, although I'm not quite certain whether his first name is Miro, if that is the policeman I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He was the secretary for All People's Defence at the level of municipality and is a Croat by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot picture the person in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Sadikovic, then Mr. Berbic, and Mr. Petrusic participated in the procurement of weapons for the aforementioned Muslim unit in the territory of the Kotor Varos Municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I call please a document which is in e-court, 2D04-0019, please. Could you be so kind, please, to show B/C/S version ERN number 00423686. It's page 3 of B/C/S version of document. And English version is page 6, please. It is bottom, number 27, Sadikovic Muhamed and Berbic Sulejman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a poor copy, but I suppose you can see that in item 27 we find Muhamed Sadikovic, and in item 28 Sulejman Berbic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have first page, please, of this document, both English and B/C/S version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you see that this is a criminal report dated the 27th of October, 1993, submitted to the military prosecutor's office against those persons specified below. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you ever talk to Mr. Sadikovic and Mr. Berbic concerning this case, these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Sadikovic and I are not on good terms. We have no communication whatsoever. As for Mr. Berbic, he works abroad, and I do not have an opportunity to meet him. If this is the person I have in mind, I believe proceedings were instituted against him before the Banja Luka court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, could you assist us? What is the witness saying about his connection with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These two persons which are on the list of criminal charges of the initial criminal proceedings are known to this witness as a member of this military formation in the region of Kotor Varos, and simply we would like to show that certain judicial actions were taken against certain number of people, like against him when he was initially brought to police station to give statements and then going so-called pre-trial criminal proceedings, simply to have this picture, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is that sufficient of a nexus to make the document admissible through him?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my idea was just to identify these two persons through -- through this witness and to have it admitted as a clear picture about the events of which this witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I share the Presiding Judge's bewilderedness here. You are showing us a document that tells us that criminal proceedings were brought against two members of a military unit that was established within the SDA in 1992. What is the relevance of this in relation to this witness and to your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The nexus and the relevance is because this witness know, among other names, these two person that I ask him, Mr. Sadikovic who was the commander of that unit, and Mr. Berbic, who was a member. Simply to confirm this fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But the witness has already at several occasions confirmed that he knew Mr. Sadikovic and that he confirmed that Mr. Sadikovic was the head of the unit. So that has already been established several times by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Another aspect of this exhibit is that we want to show that certain judicial proceedings were launched against the alleged perpetrators. For example, this witness was also a part of this procedure during the cross-examination of my learned friend when, too, his statement in police -- state security police were made. So simply it is a part of an aspect of proceedings against certain individuals in the region of Kotor Varos, simply as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, the Prosecution's stance is that there really hasn't been any relevant or probative value attached to this document. Secondly, it deals with issues and crimes that had occurred when this witness was already in custody. It's dealing with matters that occurred in -- on the 25th of July, 24th of July, and after that. He was already, on his own evidence, in the prison in Kotor Varos by that stage. So how he can comment about -- on any of the material contained in this is -- is completely unknown at this stage. The fact that he knows or may know some of the people charged or mentioned in the document doesn't make the document itself relevant. So unless there's some clearer connection to an issue in this particular case, this document shouldn't go in, at least not through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pantelic, the Chamber's of the view that this document is not admissible, at least not through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. I'll proceed. Can we go just for a while in private session, because I will mention some persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You talked about the situation in the Kotor Varos area, and you said that the larger-scale conflict began around the 11th of June, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you personally know that some actions were being prepared among the non-Serb population before the action on the 11th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any information about that. Here and there you could see that something was going on, some sort of unusual movement or night guard, guard shifts at the outskirts of the villages, but the situation was more or less usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 65 ter document from that list 689.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on the left-hand side is the version in the language that you can understand. At the bottom of the page under paragraph 3 headed "The Situation on the Ground." Can you see that on that page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And please show the witness page number 2 of the B/C/S version ERN number 00861575, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the top of that page you can see that it says that in the area there is intensive reconnaissance activity and attempts at organising an uprising of the Muslim population outside the conflict areas, particularly in the area of Bosanska Gradiska and Kotor Varos. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the bottom of that second page. And you can see that the General Momir Talic, commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, is the one who signed this document. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Show the witness, please, page 1 of this document with the headings, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the top left-hand side you can see that the document was drafted on the 8th of June, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 8th or the 10th. It says the 10th. Yes. It is -- that -- the date, the 8th of June, is typed, but then there is a correction underneath that, stating that it was the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that an uprising was being prepared in the Kotor Varos area by your compatriots. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you permit, Your Honours, this is a report of the command of the Krajina Corps, and this is their assessment. I can say that the situation was very confusing in that period, and you can conclude by what I say that for a while, since the spring, there were some disruptions and regular life was disrupted. Some companies were not working. People were not going for their regular leave. There was fear, insecurity, the constant presence of military formations that were leaving for Croatia. So the document probably was made on the basis of some assessments, but it's a document by the corps commander. I cannot deny what is stated in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can we have exhibit number for this document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Again the same questions occur as with the last document you attempted to exhibit. The -- is this -- is he -- was he a part of the -- is it his document? Was he a part of the command, for want of a better expression, that would have produced this? Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Obviously not, Your Honour, but simply this is information that this witness knows about the events, from his knowledge, of course, in territory of Kotor Varos about the armaments and operations. Simply that, which is confirmed by this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But to repeat what we said during the last discussion, the witness's testimony as to his knowledge, his experience, is what is clearly receivable. That there are documents in existence which -- the background or contents of which he is familiar does not, without more, make the document admissible as an item of evidence. And I'm asking you to indicate to us why in this case it is your submission that this document is admissible as an exhibit. For myself, I don't see it immediately, but you may be able to persuade us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Clearly -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, in accordance with your guidelines, hearsay is admissible as far as I know. So he just confirm the situation which was actually occurred in the territory of Kotor Varos. And in addition to that, this document clearly confronts certain portion of witness testimony. First of all, he is saying here that everything was more or less calm in the territory of municipality of Kotor Varos, that certain occasional incidents were -- broke out, but this particular documents, as well as the future exhibits that Defence will offer, clearly contradicts to certain portion of his statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, clearly this -- the hearsay is admissible. The witness is giving weight to a hearsay document. Now -- I'm sorry. If we are to apply the standard as I understand the Trial Chamber now to pursue, then we are going to have a huge problem with the bar table admission of documents, because we will not have -- I mean, that is the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, that the bar table documents are admitted, but the bar table documents are not -- are not introduced through a witness, just bar table documents. Now, if we have -- if we have this standard, I'm really getting concerned about the bar table admission. I mean, I was just trying to raise this point also so you have that in view during the deliberations. Thank you very much. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm not unaware of that rule in terms of admissibility, but our concern is at the end of the exercise a management problem of allowing in a large volume of paper which may at the end of the day not, in fact, be relevant. So we have to take these -- unfortunately -- I shouldn't say unfortunately. We can only deal with these questions as they arise, one at a time. There's no other way of dealing with it. And the immediate problem is that we don't see how this assists. Does the Prosecution have a view.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I mean the issue of the authenticity of the document and the relevance or probative value of the documents are also considerations that you should take into account in deciding this question. There's not much evidence at all from this witness - and I don't expect there would be - concerning the actual authenticity of the document. And so far the questioning hasn't revealed any high level of any probative value of this document insofar as this witness is concerned. He can't add anything to it or shed any light on its contents that enhance your understanding of his evidence. Perhaps a solution would be to have it marked for identification, and if the Defence want to deal with the -- try and tender the document at a later stage after more evidence has been adduced in the case or perhaps through another witness, then that might save their position and also mean that the decision is deferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, to the extent that the document speaks to attacks in the area, for that limited purpose it appears -- there appears to be some nexus, so we will admit this document, and it may be marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2D1 -- yes, that's correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- Exhibit 2D1, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, you are an expert for military engineering. Can you please tell me the village of Vecici in the Kotor Varos Municipality, what sort of fortification facilities were built by your compatriots there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the context of what event? What event does this question refer to? I apologise. I will answer gladly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the context of the conflict with Serbian forces in the territory of the Kotor Varos Municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise again, but do you have a specific date? Is it -- because before the 11th of June, there were no fortifications or barriers, only in the event of some incidents there were some improvised barricades made of fallen trees on the Kotor Varos-Banja Luka road.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in the village itself, were there any armoured reinforced cement bunkers or anything like that? Just say yes or no if you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't know about that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are familiar with the events when two -- when Milan Stevilovic, a colonel, and a high-ranking police official from the Banja Luka CSB, Stevan Markovic, were killed, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Of course I received this information and I heard this story, but I was in prison at that time. I was already in prison at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What did you hear? Who was the perpetrator of this ambush?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A group of young men carried out this ambush on the Vrbanjci-Kotor Varos road in the Rujevica hamlet. This is where this tragedy occurred, and several people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: These young men, they were Muslims, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who they were. Most probably, yes, because in that period Croats and Bosniaks were on good terms, and it could be that the group was made up both of Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in one part of the statement you provided to the Prosecutor you say that the resistance in the village of Vecici lasted for four to five months. Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It was quite strong resistance, I guess, and I assume that there were plenty of weapons there as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the events relating to the Vecici hamlet are of a tragic nature. After their attempt to get out via Travnik, a large number of people are still being considered as missing, and there is no logic to thinking that they had lots of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. All I asked was that since the resistance lasted for four to five months and since you or reserve officer and familiar with military science, how can resistance be sustained for a period of four to five months if there aren't considerable weapons? Isn't that illogical?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can sustain it in two ways, that the persons who are putting up the resistance are strong and that the persons who are carrying out the attacks are weak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us proceed. If I were to read to you the statement given by Mr. Sadikovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, could you hold on for ten seconds, please. We are going to take a break. I just want to indicate to you how much time you have left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, maximum --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maximum number 15 minutes, but I'll do my best to even make less. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we'll take a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. You may continue, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we kindly ask that we wait until all background noise in the courtroom ceases. Thank you. Could Mr. Pantelic please repeat his question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Pantelic. The interpreter is asking you to repeat your question because the noise of the blinds interrupted you. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if I read out Mr. Sadikovic's statement, who, as you confirmed, was the commander of the unit in the territory of Kotor Varos, which he gave on the 25th of June, 2003, in the Brdjanin case, where you also testified, concerning weapons ... I'll read in English since the official transcript is in English. "At that time we had automatic weapons, the members of the reserve force, for instance, had them, and they in part joined the resistance and we also had hunting weapons because we had our hunting society in Kotor Varos. There was quite a number of hunters, and people made their weapons, they would take some pipings, pipes or tubes and make something -- some sort of single-barrelled rifles or pistols with some makeshift -- a certain number of our men had worked in Croatia and Slovenia, which made explosives. So when they come home to Kotor Varos, they brought those back. So they made those devices. Or at times, they had bought the original TNT from Serbs. They bought so-called soaps [phoen], hundred-gram packages and used them to make bombs..." In addition, he said that: "We didn't have any hand-held launchers, not in the beginning. But we had zoljas, which is a smallish anti-armour device which is used to act against armoured vehicles. We didn't have Osa's at that time. They were larger, and later on we captured some of them, and we captured more machine-guns, so that later on we had more machine-guns, but this was later brought, a group of guys who were in Travnik brought these -- brought one also to Vecici. I heard that one also had me brought with three or four charges, but later on, we captured mortars..." [Interpretation] Sir, you were not privy to those events given your circumstances, but there's no reason not for you to confirm what the commander of that unit said before this Tribunal, is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A statement given under oath or before this Tribunal, for me, is something that I cannot comment as such. There would be no logic in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My question was rather simple. You agree with this statement, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the village of Sedari [phoen] is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, I am very familiar with that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mostly Serbs resided there; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was an ethnically-pure village for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That village was attacked by non-Serb forces, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I later learned that the village was attacked. I learned that only after I was released from prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of what forces attacked it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no precise information to that extent. As a person, I do not like to recall the names of all these locations which went through the worst. There is a number of such villages in Kotor Varos Municipality. I don't like revisiting that. I wish that had never happened. If I could ask for this Court's indulgence not to dwell on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I understand you fully, and we won't pursue this matter much further, but you heard of certain civilian casualties aged between 4 and 64 who were Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As of the moment I returned to Kotor Varos and in the past ten years, and by reading the media, as well as by talking to some of the survivors from that village, I began hearing of the atrocities there and the number of civilian victims, and I truly sympathise with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I fully respect what you said. You were also a municipal deputy. Therefore, you are acquainted with the decision-making mechanism in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was a deputy to the Municipal Assembly in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I read out to you that in the Brdjanin case, when asked about the functioning of the Crisis Staff, Mr. Sadikovic said the following. The question was: "What happened with respect when the Assembly could not sit and its functions were performed by a Crisis Staff. Could the Crisis Staff issue direction to the police? "A. Yes. In such instances, of course, the Municipal Assembly ceased to function. The Crisis Staff assumes all its duties, and the Crisis Staff has more jurisdiction, more competencies over other bodies, that is, and it can have its say in army or police matters too." MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, the problem with that question is that it's not clear at all, firstly, what's being put to this man who is sitting here in front of you; and, secondly, what Crisis Staff was the witness in the other case talking about? That's not clear to me. He is talking about a theoretical situation, talking about a SDA Crisis Staff or a Serb Crisis Staff, Crisis Staff in Kotor Varos, or what? And we should this sort of issue inject a lot more precision, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In my learned friend will be more patient, then he will get the answer. So the question was designed to have answer, if any, in theoretical terms. So it is not particular question regarding Kotor Varos or anything else. It's simply question, answer, and opinion of this witness because he is a member of municipal parliament, simply as that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I thought I understood you, Mr. Pantelic, until the last phrase you used about the witness giving his opinion. The -- but that apart, how is the -- the general observations he has of assistance to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In fact, one witness before this court in Brdjanin case, Mr. Sadikovic, who was also a political figure, said certain things regarding the competence of Crisis Staff. Mr. Witness is also a member of municipal municipality, so he is a representative, and he should, theoretically, have his opinion regarding the role and duty of Municipal Assembly in peacetime and Crisis Staff in wartime, simply as that. So I just want to have his opinion in very general and theoretical terms. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: But ... Your Honours, I think I know where this issue is going. It's going to be an inquiry of this witness of the theoretical powers of Crisis Staffs to issue direction to police forces back in 1992. In fact, I think that's what the commencement of the question was all about. Now, if that's what Mr. Pantelic wants to raise with the witness, then he can, and he should ask him directly. Secondly, if Mr. Pantelic wants to adduce the evidence of Mr. Sadikovic, of course he can at a later stage. And thirdly, you have issued practice directions that cross-examining -- the name of the witness -- when prior statements of a witness given in another place, another session of evidence, counsel should not mention the name of the witness, and that's a third matter of concern. The issue could simply be addressed by asking this witness if he knows what the general position was with respect to Crisis Staffs issuing directions to police back in 1992, if he's qualified, if he's qualified, to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying Mr. Pantelic's question. Mr. Pantelic, now that you have had the opportunity to have your question phrased by Defence Counsel -- by Prosecuting Counsel, could you ask the witness again? A, his competence to speak to what you're trying to get to; and, B, then what is -- what he says about it. So there are two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you tell us whether you agree with Mr. Sadikovic's statement in which he said that the Crisis Staff in wartime situations was a body which had some rather wide competencies in relation to the military and police. Do you agree with it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a deputy to the Assembly, I am aware of the fact that the Assembly is the most senior legislative body at the municipal level, as at other levels as well. The Crisis Staff formed by the municipality cannot take over the powers and competence of the Assembly. It has to be established by virtue of a decree or a document issued by the Assembly. Hence I disagree with all of the statement. In certain extraordinary circumstances a Crisis Staff can take over the role of an Assembly if it is unable to meet, but only within the purview of its own authority. This is a legal matter which was regulated by the statute of the municipality, its rules of procedure, and certain legislation which are at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you testified before this Tribunal in the Brdjanin case, when asked by Judge Janu, you spoke about the role of the young policeman who I believe was the prison warden. You said the following: "May I be allowed to say something. Because I feel it is my duty. It has happened that the prison warden, that was a young man who was a policeman, sometimes fire would be opened on him to gain access to us, but he would then stand in front of some special formation and protected us, that is, prevented them from entering the prison. They had come to the prison in a very ill faith. And I do not wish you to think bad about somebody only because he was a guard in a prison where I was kept." [Interpretation] Do you stand by your previous testimony today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My question is do you still stand by the words you uttered in the Brdjanin case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I absolutely do. I established contact with that person in the meantime, and I actually have regular contact with certain prison guards in Kotor Varos. I live there. I meet those people. And with some of them I'm even on friendly terms. The young man I referred to is Mr. Zaric, aka Ziba. In any case, I stand fully by my previous statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you might know this: Was there a detention unit in the SUP building? Were there such facilities in the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was detained temporarily in the SUP building, only in an office on the first floor. I don't know whether there was something in the basement of the building. That building was not completed at that time. I still don't think it was. Under the existing regulation of Yugoslavia, one such building needed to have a nuclear shelter, and that was supposed to be done. Unfortunately, it never was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In any case, you will agree with me that in Kotor Varos there was no official prison, no detention -- court detention unit or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The room in which I spent over a year in was precisely for that purpose, but I must say that -- as I have said already, that it was adapted to that purpose. Perhaps it had a different purpose prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I fully understand, but my question was simple. Before 1992, there was no court detention facility in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If you had been in a situation to be the commander or head of a unit arresting Serbs, where would you have placed those people? Isn't it logical that in the absence of a prison you use other facilities? Is what I'm saying logical?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am more than happy that I was never in a situation to have to arrest anyone. I never even thought about such issues, not even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But I'm just asking you this: If there is no official prison, there's no room, so why not come up with another facility such as a TO building, school buildings, factory buildings? This is what I'm asking you. Does this make sense what I'm asking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Defence Counsel, I understand fully, but, to me, most of the things which took place at that time in that area were illogical. Do not ask me what I would have done had some been arrested. I can only thank God that I was never put in such a position to arrest anyone. I don't know what would have been. I simply was not in such a situation, and that would be my final answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I fully understand, Witness, but my question was directed at you as a technical person, an engineer who would presumably understand the conditions, but let's move on to another topic. Tell me this, would you agree with me that the following facts emerged from your today's testimony: One, you are a well-trained military officer with more than an average knowledge about weapons and explosives. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Second fact: Much before the 11th of June, 1992, with a great number of your compatriots and Croatian neighbours, you planned an armed conflict with the Serbs in the municipality covered by Kotor Varos. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because of such circumstances, you were arrested, brought in. You provided statements to the police, and a pre-trial proceedings were instituted against you. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I fail to understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's a simple question, really. You were arrested. You gave statements to the police because there was suspicion that you took part in the organised resistance against the Serb population in Kotor Varos. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If you had not been arrested and if you had been in Commander Sadikovic's unit, would you have killed Serbs as a member of that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would you have carried out sabotage incidents such as planting explosive -- explosives which may have resulted in civilian casualties? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. This is not my witness, but I had requested from your legal officers if I could have five minutes at the end of the day to raise procedural matters concerning the next two witnesses coming that I think we need resolved. He's already gone over his time limit. I would ask if we could intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Three minutes, Your Honours, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, which forces killed hundreds upon hundreds of Serbs in Kotor Varos Municipality? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who roasted living Serbs in Kotor Varos Municipality? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who burned and levelled the Serb villages in the territory of Kotor Varos Municipality? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. Re-examination? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I know that the issue that my colleague Mr. Hannis wants to raise with you is of the utmost importance to the Prosecution. Could -- could I respectfully ask you to deal with that before I proceed to any re-examination? It may be that -- it may be that there won't be any need for re-examination, but I would ask that you allow Mr. Hannis the time to address you on that. It's a matter of crucial importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Two matters. One regards Witness ST-56 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is it in relation to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, not this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In that case I suggest we take it the other way around. I understood from your colleagues that your input now was in relation to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. MR. DI FAZIO: In that case if Your Honours please, I have no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Witness, I have just one issue that I would like to raise with you. Because right in the beginning of your testimony today you mentioned that you were on your way down to the river and that you crossed the river on the bridge in order to establish contacts with a gentleman who you named as Mr. Slobodan Zupljanin. Now, who was that actually, and why did you wish to establish contact with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, for several reasons. First, I knew him personally. He used to be a manager in a local company. I heard from some people that he was in the command and that he was a person of authority. I wanted to talk to him to try and discuss the grave situation in which weapons were used and find a solution. That was my motive, none other. Of course, there were refugees who had left their homes, and they wanted someone, which happened to be me, to have that conversation so that military activities would stop and that people would be allowed to leave the area for certain other parts of the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the nature of the authority which Mr. Slobodan Zupljanin held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time what his precise authority was, but I do know that he was in charge of a regular TO unit in Kotor Varos Municipality. It existed until the 11th of June, 1992. It was a reserve JNA unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So just to make sure that the gentleman you were seeking to establish contact with is different from one of the accused in this trial, Mr. Stojan Zupljanin. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one matter of the transcript, Your Honour. It's page 78, 23. I believe the witness said he used "to be" a manager in a local company, not "to have."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So the witness may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you for your attendance and your assistance to the Tribunal, and you may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The first matter deals with the next witness that we intend to call, who is ST-56. There was a request for protective measures. In your decision, you indicated that this witness would be given a pseudonym and that you found that it was appropriate to have facial and voice distortion. But in the order, you only ordered facial distortion. So we -- we needed to clarify whether or not she was going to be permitted to have voice distortion as well, because, as you know, it takes additional time to set that up technically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And she is requesting voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: She is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So the decision of the Chamber in that regard is that she be afforded both facial and voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. The second matter relates to the third witness to come, who is ST-27, and there are two matters. Ms. Korner, I think, sent an e-mail request to Ms. Featherstone yesterday or the day before concerning changing the mode of testimony for him. He was originally proposed as a viva voce witness. Upon further review of his transcript and other matters, she proposed to change his mode of testimony to 92 ter, and it would help in our planning and scheduling if we can know the Trial Chamber's position on that. And related to that there's the issue of protective measures for him. He had recently had protective measures in the Brdjanin case. It's my understanding that the jurisprudence here in the Trial Chamber that those protective measures remain in place to future cases absent a specific finding. He is also a witness in another case for which he has not requested protective measures, and those have been removed for that case. It's our position, however, absent a specific request to remove the original protective measures from the Brdjanin case for this witness, they remain in effect for this case, and we would request that be the situation. He has indicated to us that he does want those previous protective measures in this case. And we think there is precedent here where witnesses have had protective measures in one case and not in another because their specific security -- their specific security concerns pertain often times to the individual accused, the present location of the witness, the present location of friends and fans of the accused in that case, etc. And we think under the circumstances that absent a specific finding by you or the previous Trial Chambers that those protective measures should remain in effect for ST-27 in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, first about the protective measures, we -- we stated in our joint reply our position. We think that it's -- that it lacks any rationale, that the same witness has the protective measures in one case, and in the other case he says, "I don't need the protective measures." I really don't think that the Prosecution and the witness should be accommodated in that respect. That's the essence of our submission, which is already filed. The second thing, Your Honour, we believe the -- the changing of the witness on such a short notice from viva voce to 92 ter creates -- creates a huge prejudice to the Defence. Basically according to the rules which Your Honours -- instructions which Your Honours gave to us, the viva voce witnesses would come, would testify, and his testimony and the exhibits that are -- that he -- that are tendered through him becomes a part of the record. Now we are preparing our cross-examination on the basis of that. Now in 24 hours before we are notified that the OTP wants to change it to 92 ter, which means that his previous transcripts, previous exhibits in other cases, and all that is coming in. We're simply not prepared, and we can't be prepared for that. And I don't think that this is the proper way to -- I mean, this is a short -- I know it is up to the party to choose which way will they present their evidence and their witnesses, but this such a short notice really creates a prejudice for the Defence, and we will not be able to cross-examine the witness based on the case that he's a 92 ter witness. Thank you, Your Honours. That's all I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just for the record that Zupljanin Defence fully support the submission of Mr. Zecevic, and in addition to that, please, we kindly beg you to exercise your authority over the OTP in this absolutely unsustainable practice, because this is a serious violation of the rights of the accused. Twenty-four hours before the witness coming changing of the mode of testimony, simply unbearable. Thank you so much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you had something to add in response to Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Pantelic's objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, if I may. Just for clarity of the record, it's not 24 hours before the witness is coming that the notice was given. Ms. Korner e-mailed the parties and legal officer at 2.41 yesterday afternoon. So even if he were to come on sometime tomorrow, it would be more like 44 hours. However, we have two other witnesses before him scheduled now. Given the rate at which we proceeded on the witness today, it may be that he won't come on until the day after tomorrow. And I think allowing the Prosecution to make this change does serve -- warrant interest of the Trial Chamber to have the Prosecution's case to conclude sooner because it will take less time with the 92 ter than with the viva voce witness thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, the Trial Chamber certainly appreciates any method adopted by counsel to shorten the actual court time involved in these matters. But in this case we take Defence counsel at their word, that they are prejudiced by the change of method proposed by the Prosecution. So what we would respectfully suggest to the -- to the Prosecution is that in -- in future cases when such a change is proposed that a longer period of notice be given to the other side. But as I said, the Chamber's appreciative of the attempts to shorten the actual court time devoted to this. So in this case we -- the motion is -- the application is refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And on Ms. Korner's behalf, may I inquire if this witness were to be rescheduled at a later date, might the Chamber's ruling be different? If he were to come first thing next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. Hannis. As the Presiding Judge has just said, the Chamber really wishes to encourage both parties to find ways to shorten the trial time. And so changing the status of a witness from viva voce to 92 ter is something that the Chamber is very happy to see, and we will accommodate that wherever possible. Now, in this case we just think that the notice was too short. If, as you suggest you want to put off ST-27 to a later date and then re-introduce him as a 65 -- as a 92 ter witness, that's fine, but again we wouldn't gain any time because we would then lose the time that we have for him now. I am not aware of any witnesses that you have brought for Friday; is that correct? Oh, do you have witnesses for Friday?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Perhaps I can be of assistance. The -- this witness is scheduled to testify late tomorrow, if we get to him, and Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And he's the only witness to testify Friday?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes. Depending on the length of time the first two witnesses take tomorrow will depend whether we reach him or not tomorrow, but he is the own scheduled -- he is the only one for the rest of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But ahead of him we have -- yes, we have two other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: There are two other witnesses ahead of him. And we had an indication from the Defence as to how long they will take to cross-examine the first witness informally today, but we don't have yet an indication of how long they would take to cross-examine the second witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I was just coming to that. I think we will proceed as scheduled, namely to hear to -- now he's here to hear him now, but hear him viva voce. The Prosecution, if I recall well, has three hours. If you wish to shave some time off that, you can do it. But I think in the end, it's the most practical thing to keep him here and have him testify this time as viva voce. I was just about to ask the Defence teams if they could be good enough to indicate to us the time that they would wish to have for their cross-examination of the next witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we indicated to our colleagues, as far as the Stanisic Defence is concerned, that we intend to cross-examine the next two witnesses at 15 minutes each at the most. And the rest of the time, which I -- which according to my calculation is one hour and 20 minutes for the -- for the ST-27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: One hour and 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for ST-27. I think. I mean, depending how long we will take between these two coming witnesses, because we said, Your Honour, two hours altogether for four witnesses. That's roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the next witness we planned some 20 minutes. For ST-27, we plan to use the rest of our hour and a half. So an hour and 15 minutes or an hour and ten minutes as needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you to both of you. Hold on one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krkovic, can I just clarify with you that you would wish to use 20 minutes for the next two witnesses? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. With a bit of luck, it looks in my schedule as if we should be able to finish of VS -- ST, sorry, ST-27 by the end of Friday. So I think that's the best way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: On the 22nd September, Prosecutor filed a motion requesting that protective measures remain in place for ST-027. Trial Chamber will ask ST-027 to explain the reasons for requesting protective measures once he is in court. On 25th of September, the Prosecution filed a motion for leave to amend the exhibit list to add four documents related to the same witness. The Defence jointly objected to this motion on the 28th of September. Contrary to the Prosecution's submission, at the time the Prosecution's exhibit list was filed on 8th of June, 2009, ST-27 did not benefit from the protective measures of delayed disclosure of his identity. Those protective measures were varied by the Appeals Chamber in the decision of the 21st April, 2005, in Brdjanin, to permit immediate disclosure of 27 -- ST-27's identity to Mico Stanisic. The Prosecution acknowledged this in its filing of a corrigendum to its pre-trial brief on the 22nd of June, 2009. The Prosecution disclosed the documents to the Defence at that time within the deadline set by the Pre-Trial Judge. However, the Prosecution did not at that time seek to amend its exhibit list, but instead waited more than three months until approximately a week prior to the witness's testimony to do so. The Prosecutor has offered no explanation for not seeking to amend his exhibit list when it realised that the witness was no longer entitled to delayed disclosure. In the Trial Chamber's opinion, the Defence has not had adequate notice of the Prosecution's intention to rely on these documents at trial, and the Trial Chamber considers that the Prosecution has not shown good cause for its request to amend the exhibit list at this point in time. The Chamber is further not persuaded that the documents are of sufficient importance to justify delayed inclusion on the exhibit list. The motion is therefore denied.
